description: We’re Team Zenon, and we’re heading to the Moon’s south pole, the target for the next generation of commercial landers and Artemis missions. Light, shadow and communication decide whether a mission there succeeds or fails. Using NASA lighting, terrain and orbital data, we’re building a planning tool that turns that complexity into clear, confident decisions for mission teams. Engineering, robotics, AI and business thinking, built to perfection.
summary:
At the lunar south pole, the Sun never rises more than 1.5° above the horizon, casting massive, slow-moving shadows. For solar-powered rovers, driving the "shortest path" often means driving into the dark, freezing, and failing the mission.

We built Sunchaser, a mission-planning platform that goes far beyond the minimum requirements of the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. By combining real NASA JPL ephemerides and LRO LOLA terrain data, Sunchaser computes hour-by-hour sunlight and Earth visibility.

Our core innovation is a Space-Time A* rover planner. Instead of just asking where to drive, our AI asks when to drive. It treats the rover's time and battery state as part of the map, allowing it to detour or park in the sunlight to survive moving shadows. We validate our routes using Monte Carlo simulations to prove survival probabilities against real-world hardware uncertainties.

In our demo scenario (Slater Plain), a standard shortest route froze after 17 hours (10% survival). Sunchaser's route detoured through sunlit ground, arriving safely with a 100% survival probability. Sunchaser turns raw NASA data into actionable, life-saving decisions for commercial lunar missions.
details:
Sunchaser is an interactive web planner that answers the three questions every lunar south-pole mission faces: where to land, when to land, and how to keep a solar rover alive.

At the south pole the Sun never climbs more than about 1.5° above the horizon. It circles the sky once every 29.5 days, so even small hills cast shadows kilometres long that never stop moving. One crater rim can stay lit for weeks while ground nearby is dark for days. A solar lander or rover that ends up in shadow loses power, burns its battery on heaters and freezes. Earth also sits low on the horizon, so terrain can cut off direct-to-Earth radio for days at a time.

We built Sunchaser on NASA data. For each of NASA's nine Artemis III candidate regions, we computed the Sun's and Earth's positions for every hour of 2027 (8,760 hours) using JPL Horizons. We then ray-cast the real terrain horizon in 720 directions out to 150 km from LRO LOLA elevation maps, correcting for lunar curvature. From this, Sunchaser works out how much of the Sun's disk is visible each hour, whether Earth is in view, and when a Deep Space Network station can see the Moon.

Sunchaser then turns this data into decisions:

- Where: it ranks the nine sites by usable days, each needing at least 12 hours of sunlight and 4 hours of Earth contact. In June 2027, Peak near Cabeus B gives 10 out of 10 usable days.

- When: it scores every possible landing time in 2027, every six hours. Depending on the site, only 14–54% of landing times are survivable, so timing matters as much as place.

- How: it plans rover routes across real 5 km terrain maps with sunlight computed for every hour. The planner searches position, time and battery together, so it can detour through sunlight or wait for a shadow to pass, and it never drops below a 15% battery reserve. Each route is replayed 500 times with uncertain battery, panel output and power draw. The shortest route freezes at 7 of 9 sites. At Slater Plain it survives 10% of runs, while Sunchaser's route survives 100%.

The website shows all of this through a 3D Moon built from LROC imagery, 3D terrain draped with real LROC photos and lit by the real Sun direction, landing-window calendars, and a business model that turns a mission budget into cost per usable day and shows what a launch slip costs. A Google Gemini copilot answers questions in plain English, and every number it gives about our sites is checked against the computed data.

We validated our results against NASA. Our sunlight and Earth visibility correlate 0.98 and 0.99 with NASA's published LOLA illumination maps, and the model reproduces the conditions at the real IM-1 and IM-2 landing sites.

Sunchaser matters because commercial landers are going to the south pole now, each with a fixed budget and limited days on the surface. The right site, date and route can be the difference between a full mission and a frozen robot.
